<!-- docs/en/guides/troubleshooting.md -->

# Troubleshooting

Production settings refuse to start on unsafe or missing configuration, and say which variable to
fix. This page maps each refusal to its cause.

## The minimum production environment

| Variable | Why |
|---|---|
| `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY`, `PRIVACY_HMAC_KEY`, `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` | Three different random secrets: `python scripts/generate_production_secrets.py` |
| `FIELD_ENCRYPTION_ACTIVE_KEY_ID`, `FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEYS` | The key ring (same script) |
| `DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, `DJANGO_CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS`, `DJANGO_CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` | Your hosts; origins are `https://` |
| `PUBLIC_URL` | `https://app.example.com`: base of every link we e-mail |
| `DATABASE_URL` or `DB_*` | PostgreSQL, TLS with certificate checking (`sslmode=verify-full`) |
| `REDIS_URL` | `rediss://`; carries sessions, lockout and throttles |
| `TRUSTED_PROXY_COUNT` or `TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS` | How the app is reached; without it every client looks like the proxy |
| `S3_BUCKET` | Uploads and exports (or `OBJECT_STORAGE_REQUIRED=false` with a persistent volume) |
| `SENTRY_DSN` or `SENTRY_ENABLED=false` | Error reporting, or an explicit no |
| `EMAIL_HOST` ... | A real mail backend |
| `PRIVACY_CONTROLLER_NAME`, `DPO_EMAIL` or `DPO_CONTACT_URL` | Who is responsible and the channel to them |

## "ImproperlyConfigured: ..." at start-up

| Message begins | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `... looks like a placeholder` / `has too little variety` | A secret copied from an example. Generate real ones |
| `... must differ from ...` | Two secrets are equal |
| `Production database must use TLS` / `sslmode=require ... never checks` | Use `sslmode=verify-full`; on a private network you control set `DB_ALLOW_INSECURE_TRANSPORT=true` (or `DB_ALLOW_UNVERIFIED_TLS=true` to keep `require`) |
| `REDIS_URL must use rediss://` | Use TLS, or `REDIS_ALLOW_INSECURE=true` on a private network |
| `Declare how the app is reached` | Set `TRUSTED_PROXY_COUNT`/`TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS`, or `TRUSTED_PROXY_DIRECT=true` |
| `Production object storage is required` | Set `S3_BUCKET` |
| `SENTRY_DSN is required` | Give a DSN or `SENTRY_ENABLED=false` |
| `PUBLIC_URL must be the https origin` | `https://host`, no path |
| `Set PRIVACY_CONTROLLER_NAME` / `Set DPO_EMAIL or DPO_CONTACT_URL` | Publish who answers for personal data |
| `Production Temporal needs sealed payloads` / `must use TLS` | Keep `TEMPORAL_PAYLOAD_ENCRYPTION=true`; TLS or an API key, or `TEMPORAL_ALLOW_INSECURE=true` on a private network |
| `ADMIN_ENABLED in production requires ADMIN_ALLOWED_IPS` | Name the networks that may reach `/admin/` |

## Symptoms

| You see | Look at |
|---|---|
| Sign-in works but `/admin/` answers 403 `mfa_required` | Staff need an authenticator first (`/accounts/2fa/`) |
| `403 mfa_required` or "must enable two-factor" on organization endpoints | `ORG_PRIVILEGED_MFA_REQUIRED` in production: enrol an authenticator |
| `403 reauthentication_required` creating a key | Sign in again; the window is `APIKEY_REQUIRE_RECENT_AUTH_SECONDS` |
| Every user shares one rate limit or lockout | The proxy is not declared correctly (`doctor` -> client ip) |
| `429` from `/mcp` | `MCP_RATE_PER_MINUTE_IP`; many agents behind one address |
| Webhook endpoint refused with `blocked_address` | The URL resolves to a non-public address (the SSRF guard) |
| Uploads fail with `scanner_unavailable` | `UPLOAD_CLAMAV_ADDR` is set and unreachable; fix it or set `UPLOAD_CLAMAV_REQUIRED=false` knowingly |
| `audit_verify` reports a break | See the audit runbook in [Runbooks](../deploy/runbooks.md) |
| `doctor` warns "the runtime role can rewrite the audit trail" | Connect as a role that does not own the schema ([Hardening](../security/hardening.md)) |
| OAuth client cannot register | `OAUTH_DCR_ANONYMOUS`, or its redirect URI is neither `https` nor loopback |
| The image says OpenTelemetry is missing | Build with `--build-arg EXTRAS="--extra otel"` |

Anything else: `python manage.py doctor --strict`, then the logs (JSON, one line per event,
carrying `request_id`).


---

<!-- docs/en/guides/upgrading.md -->

# Upgrading from upstream

Your product started as a copy of this template. The template keeps improving (security fixes
above all), and you want those without losing your work.

## Keep the seam clean

- Your code lives in **your apps** (`src/apps/<yours>/`), added to `LOCAL_APPS`. Avoid editing the
  platform apps (`actions`, `accounts`, `audit`, `privacy`, `organizations`, ...): extend through
  the discovery files (`actions.py`, `events.py`, `privacy.py`, ...) and settings.
- When you must change a platform file, keep the change small and comment why; it is where merge
  conflicts will happen.
- Do not rename the Python packages. `scripts/init_project.py` renames the product, not the imports,
  for exactly this reason.

## The routine

```bash
git remote add template <template url>      # once
git fetch template
git merge template/main                      # or: git rebase template/main
python scripts/verify.py                     # the whole gate
```

1. Read the new `CHANGELOG.md` entries first, especially **Security** and **Breaking**.
2. Conflicts cluster in `README`, settings, docs and `pyproject.toml`. Keep your product's
   identity, take the template's behaviour.
3. Regenerate: `python manage.py actions_catalog`, `python scripts/check_openapi.py --write`,
   `python scripts/gen_docs.py`.
4. `python manage.py makemigrations --check` must be clean; apply new migrations in staging first.
5. Re-read `SECURITY.md` and `docs/en/security/review.md`: new controls sometimes need a setting.

## Migrations and data formats

Template migrations are additive within a minor release. A release that changes a data format says
so under **Breaking** and ships the command (for example `reencrypt_fields` after a key or scheme
change). Roll back the image, never the database.

## Releases and the image

Tag `vX.Y.Z` in **your** repository. The release workflow runs the full gate, scans and signs the
image and attaches provenance and an SBOM. Deploy by the digest it prints, not the tag. To verify a
signature: `cosign verify <image>@<digest> --certificate-identity-regexp '...' --certificate-oidc-issuer
https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`.

## When to take a fix immediately

A `Security` entry in the template's changelog, or an advisory in a dependency (`pip-audit` runs
weekly in CI). Merge, run the gate, release.


---

<!-- docs/en/guides/uploads.md -->

# Uploads

`POST /api/v1/uploads/` (multipart, scope `uploads:write`), `GET /api/v1/uploads/<id>/download/`.

What is checked, in order: the organization's quota (`QUOTA_UPLOAD_FILES_PER_ORG`,
`QUOTA_UPLOAD_BYTES_PER_ORG`), size (`UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES`, below the request body cap), extension in
`UPLOAD_ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS`, every dotted segment (so `x.php.png` fails), the content against the
extension (magic bytes; text must be UTF-8 without NUL), office/zip files for entry count, expanded
size, compression ratio, unsafe paths and encryption. HTML, SVG and executable types are never
allowed.

The storage key never contains the client's name; the served content type is the sniffed one;
downloads are attachments with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and a sandbox CSP.

Optional antivirus: `UPLOAD_CLAMAV_ADDR=host:port` (clamd). When set, an unreachable scanner
refuses uploads unless `UPLOAD_CLAMAV_REQUIRED=false`. The connection to clamd is plain TCP: keep
it on a private network.

## Storage

Local disk by default. For any S3-compatible store (AWS S3, MinIO, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2) set:

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `S3_BUCKET` | The bucket (production requires it, or `OBJECT_STORAGE_REQUIRED=false` with a persistent volume) |
| `S3_ENDPOINT_URL` | For non-AWS stores |
| `S3_REGION`, `S3_ADDRESSING_STYLE` | As the store requires |
| `AWS_MEDIA_KMS_KEY_ID` | Server-side encryption with KMS, optional |

Credentials come from the standard AWS variables or the platform identity (IAM role, workload
identity). The older names `BUCKET_NAME`, `AWS_MEDIA_BUCKET`, `AWS_REGION` and
`AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3` still work.

## Erasure and retention

Files are tenant-scoped and audited (`upload.created/downloaded/deleted`). When a row is deleted by
**any** path (the API, a data-subject erasure, the retention sweep) a `post_delete` hook removes the
stored file, but only if the database change commits. Retention for uploads follows the
`product-content` purpose (`retention_field` is `created_at`). A file already removed from the
bucket by hand is not an error.

Backups of the bucket are your responsibility and expire on your schedule; say so in the privacy
notice.


---

<!-- docs/en/guides/webhooks.md -->

# Webhooks

Outbound events with a transactional outbox: an event is written in the same transaction as the
change it announces, so a rollback never sends it and a commit never loses it.

```python
# <app>/events.py
register_event("order.paid", "An order was paid. Data: order_id.")
# inside the transaction that changes the order
emit("order.paid", ctx.organization, {"order_id": str(order.id)})
```

Events are **thin**: ids, not documents. A receiver fetches data with its own credentials.

## Receiving

Headers: `X-Webhook-Id` (stable across retries: deduplicate on it), `X-Webhook-Timestamp`,
`X-Webhook-Signature: v1=<hex>` where the value is HMAC-SHA256 of `"<timestamp>.<body>"` with the
endpoint secret. Reject timestamps older than a few minutes. During secret rotation two
signatures are sent (space separated); accept either.

## Managing

`/api/v1/webhooks/endpoints/` (owners/admins): create (secret returned once), update, rotate
(`rotate-secret`), send a test (`test`). `/api/v1/webhooks/deliveries/` lists history and
`redeliver`s. Endpoints must be https and resolve to public addresses.

## Delivery

Workflow with backoff 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 6h, 24h (or the `webhooks.dispatch_due` job when Temporal
is off). A claim lock prevents double sends. After `WEBHOOK_DISABLE_AFTER` consecutive failures
the endpoint is switched off and an audit event is recorded.

## SSRF protection

`apps.common.netguard` is used for every outbound call: https only, every resolved address must
be globally routable (private ranges, carrier-grade NAT, cloud metadata and tunnelled forms such as
NAT64 or 6to4 wrappers of a private IPv4 are refused), the connection goes to the validated IP (no
DNS rebinding), redirects are never followed, no proxy from the environment is used, the call has
a total deadline, and responses are size-bounded and never decompressed. A per-organization quota
limits the number of endpoints (`QUOTA_WEBHOOK_ENDPOINTS_PER_ORG`).

# Actions and MCP tools

> Generated by `python scripts/gen_docs.py`. Do not edit by hand.

| Action | MCP tool | Scope | Writes | Channels | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `actions.changes` | `actions_changes` | `actions:read` | no | api, cli, flow, mcp | List the caller's recent changes, newest first, with ids that `actions.undo` accepts. |
| `actions.undo` | `actions_undo` | `actions:write` | yes | api, cli, flow, mcp | Take back one of your own changes. Refuses if the record was edited after it. |
| `agent.report` | `agent_report` | `actions:write` | yes | mcp | Attach a summary and your model name to the current working session (optional). |
| `flags.evaluate` | `flags_evaluate` | `flags:read` | no | api, cli, flow, mcp | Which feature flags are on for you in this organization. |
| `flows.cancel` | `flows_cancel` | `flows:write` | yes | api, cli, flow, mcp | Cancel a running flow (Temporal engine only). |
| `flows.catalog` | `flows_catalog` | `flows:read` | no | api, cli, mcp | Which engine runs flows here, which flows exist, and what each engine can and cannot do. |
| `flows.runs` | `flows_runs` | `flows:read` | no | api, cli, flow, mcp | List recent flow runs of this organization. |
| `flows.signal` | `flows_signal` | `flows:write` | yes | api, cli, flow, mcp | Send a signal to a running flow (Temporal engine only). |
| `flows.start` | `flows_start` | `flows:write` | yes | api, cli, flow, mcp | Start one of the flows marked startable. Safe to call with an Idempotency-Key. |
| `flows.status` | `flows_status` | `flows:read` | no | api, cli, flow, mcp | Current status of one run (refreshed from Temporal when that engine ran it). |
| `notes.archive` | `notes_archive` | `notes:write` | yes | api, cli, flow, mcp | Archive a note. Archived notes are hidden from the default list and read-only. |
| `notes.create` | `notes_create` | `notes:write` | yes | api, cli, flow, mcp | Create a note. Send an Idempotency-Key to make retries safe. |
| `notes.get` | `notes_get` | `notes:read` | no | api, cli, flow, mcp | Read one note by id. |
| `notes.list` | `notes_list` | `notes:read` | no | api, cli, flow, mcp | List the organization's notes, newest first. |
| `notes.update` | `notes_update` | `notes:write` | yes | api, cli, flow, mcp | Change a note's title or body. Archived notes cannot be edited. |
| `settings.get` | `settings_get` | `flags:read` | no | api, cli, flow, mcp | The effective value of a runtime setting for this organization. |

| POST | `/api/v1/webhooks/endpoints/{id}/test{format}` | webhooks_endpoints_test_formatted_create |
| DELETE | `/api/v1/webhooks/endpoints/{id}{format}` | webhooks_endpoints_formatted_destroy |
| GET | `/api/v1/webhooks/endpoints/{id}{format}` | webhooks_endpoints_formatted_retrieve |
| PATCH | `/api/v1/webhooks/endpoints/{id}{format}` | webhooks_endpoints_formatted_partial_update |
| GET | `/api/v1/webhooks/endpoints{format}` | webhooks_endpoints_formatted_list |
| POST | `/api/v1/webhooks/endpoints{format}` | webhooks_endpoints_formatted_create |

<!-- docs/en/reference/engines.md -->

# Flow engines

> Generated by `python scripts/gen_docs.py`. Do not edit by hand.

| Capability | Local engine | Temporal |
|---|---|---|
| Start a flow and read its result | yes | yes |
| Run on the caller's thread vs. in a worker process | inline | worker |
| Automatic retries with backoff | no | yes |
| Survives a process restart mid-flow | no | yes |
| Durable timers and sleeps (hours to months) | no | yes |
| Signals to a running flow | no | yes |
| Queries, child workflows, continue-as-new | no | yes |
| Cancel a running flow | no | yes |
| Scheduled jobs | manage.py run_scheduler (one replica) or cron + run_job | Temporal Schedules |
| Visibility UI and history | no | yes |

| `SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT` | `'production'` | string |   | `production.py` |
| `SENTRY_RELEASE` |   | string |   | `production.py` |
| `SERVER_EMAIL` | `DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL` | string |   | `base.py` |
| `SESSION_COOKIE_AGE_SECONDS` | `43200` | integer |   | `base.py` |
| `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE` | `'Lax'` | string | "Lax" assumes the browser client is same-site. A SPA served from a different site needs "None" (which production enforces alongside Secure) or the session cookie is never sent with the cross-site XHR. | `base.py` |
| `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE` | `True` | boolean | Secure by default; local.py relaxes this for plain-HTTP development and production.py pins it True. A new settings module thus cannot silently ship insecure cookies. | `base.py` |
| `SIGNUP_ENABLED` | `False` | boolean | Accounts (django-allauth). Email is the only identity; the user model has no username. Signup is closed unless SIGNUP_ENABLED=true; new addresses must be verified before login. | `base.py` |
| `STAFF_MFA_REQUIRED` | `True` | boolean | Staff need an authenticator before the admin opens; owners and administrators before they manage a tenant (production turns the second on). A key outlives a session, so minting one needs a sign-in no older than this many seconds (0 disables), and a password or second-factor reset revokes the owner's keys. | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_ACTIVITY_THREADS` | `8` | integer |   | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_ADDRESS` | `'localhost:7233'` | string |   | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_ALLOW_INSECURE` | `False` | boolean |   | `production.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_PAYLOADS` | `False` | boolean | Read payloads that are not sealed. Only for draining histories written before encryption was on: with it off, an unsealed payload is refused, which is what stops a stranger on the Temporal network from starting an activity with an input of their choosing. | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_API_KEY` |   | string |   | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_CALL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `15` | integer |   | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_ENABLED` | `False` | boolean | Durable flows and background jobs (apps.flows). Off by default: flows then run on the local engine and tasks run inline, so a fresh clone needs nothing but the database. | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_METRICS_PORT` | `0` | integer |   | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE` | `'default'` | string |   | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_PAYLOAD_ENCRYPTION` | `True` | boolean | Seal every payload in workflow history with the field-encryption key ring. | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS` | `25` | integer |   | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_TASK_QUEUE` | `f'{deployment_name}-main'` | string |   | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_TLS` | `False` | boolean |   | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_TLS_CLIENT_CERT` |   | string |   | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_TLS_CLIENT_KEY` |   | string |   | `base.py` |
| `TEMPORAL_TLS_SERVER_CA` |   | string |   | `base.py` |
| `TEST_USE_EXTERNAL_SERVICES` | `False` | boolean |   | `test.py` |
| `TRUSTED_PROXY_COUNT` | `0` | integer |   | `base.py` |
| `TRUSTED_PROXY_DIRECT` | `False` | boolean |   | `production.py` |
| `TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS` |   | list | Host-agnostic client-IP resolution (see apps.common.network.client_ip). Set whichever matches the deployment; both default to trusting only the direct peer. | `base.py` |
| `UPLOAD_ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS` | `('pdf', 'png', 'jpg', 'jpeg', 'gif', 'webp', 'txt', 'csv', 'docx', 'xlsx')` | list |   | `base.py` |
| `UPLOAD_CLAMAV_ADDR` | `''` | string | host:port of a clamd daemon; empty disables scanning. When set, an unreachable scanner refuses the upload unless UPLOAD_CLAMAV_REQUIRED=false. | `base.py` |
| `UPLOAD_CLAMAV_REQUIRED` | `True` | boolean |   | `base.py` |
| `UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES` | `8 * 1024 * 1024` | integer | Secure uploads. The limit must stay below DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE (the body cap, which also covers multipart overhead). Extensions are matched against the sniffed content. | `base.py` |
| `UPLOAD_MAX_UNCOMPRESSED_BYTES` | `100 * 1024 * 1024` | integer |   | `base.py` |
| `UPLOAD_MAX_ZIP_ENTRIES` | `2000` | integer |   | `base.py` |
| `UPLOAD_MAX_ZIP_RATIO` | `100` | integer |   | `base.py` |
| `WEBHOOK_DISABLE_AFTER` | `50` | integer | Consecutive failed deliveries after which an endpoint is switched off. | `base.py` |

<!-- docs/en/security/audit-integrity.md -->

# Audit integrity

Each organization (plus one system chain) has its own hash chain. A row stores an **HMAC** of the
previous hash and its canonical content, keyed by `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` (held in the environment, not
the database); inserts take a PostgreSQL advisory lock as their last statement so chains stay linear
under concurrency. The consent history is chained the same way.

- Foreign keys to actors and organizations are plain ids (no constraint): deleting a user or an
  organization never touches the trail.
- A trigger rejects `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `TRUNCATE`. The only sanctioned delete is the
  `audit_prune()` function used by retention, and the trigger honours it only for the role that owns
  the table. The runtime role holds `INSERT` and `SELECT` on the table and `EXECUTE` on the function
  (`AUDIT_RUNTIME_ROLE`); it cannot update, delete, truncate or disable anything.
  Pruning writes an **anchor** row that keeps the chain verifiable after old rows go
  (`AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS`, default 365, 0 = keep forever).
- A `CHECK` constraint refuses a row without `seq` or `hash`, so a forged insert cannot sit outside
  the chain.
- Metadata is validated by key fragment and scanned with the redaction patterns; personal data does
  not belong in the trail. Failed sign-ins are coalesced per account and capped per client address;
  refused actions are capped per credential, so a caller cannot choose how fast the table grows.
- `python manage.py audit_verify [--org ID]` recomputes chains and exits non-zero on a break. The
  daily job `maintenance.verify_audit` does the same and logs each chain's head (`audit_head`).

## The newest rows

A chain proves what precedes its head: deleting the newest events leaves a shorter chain that still
verifies. Record the heads where the database cannot reach and check against them:

```bash
python manage.py audit_verify --json > heads.json      # or collect the audit_head log lines
python manage.py audit_verify --expect heads.json      # fails with "newest events are missing"
```

## What it does not defend against

The table owner or a database superuser who also holds `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY`. Separate the database
roles ([Deploy](../deploy/overview.md#two-database-identities)), keep the key in a secret manager
the database host cannot read, and ship head lines to write-once storage. `manage.py doctor` warns
when the runtime role owns the table or can modify it.

A broken chain means rows were changed outside the application. Treat it as an incident: see the
[runbooks](../deploy/runbooks.md).

<!-- docs/en/security/builder-checklist.md -->

# Builder's checklist: security and LGPD for every change

Run through the section that matches what you are adding. Each line says what to do and what
enforces it, so you know which items a green gate already covers.

## A new model

- [ ] Tenant data subclasses `OrganizationScopedModel` (test: every organization column is scoped or
      explained).
- [ ] `<app>/privacy.py`: `personal(...)` with every personal-looking field listed, or
      `not_personal(..., "why")` (tests: `test_lgpd`, `test_catalog_lint`).
- [ ] Free text that can hold personal data is `EncryptedTextField`; sensitive and child data must be.
- [ ] You know the purpose, the erase rule and the retention clock (`lgpd_check` walks you through).
- [ ] Added an index for the way you query (always `organization` first).

## A new action or endpoint

- [ ] Reads through `ctx.scoped` / `ctx.get`; never `Model.objects` (AST test).
- [ ] Docstring written for the model that reads it; scope; `write` / `destructive` / `undoable`
      declared (import-time check); `roles=` if only some roles may.
- [ ] Input is a pydantic model with bounds (`max_length`, `ge`, `le`); output never carries a
      field named like a secret (conformance test).
- [ ] Refusals are `DomainError`s with a caller-readable message.
- [ ] A test for the scope, a read-only role and another tenant (the conformance suite does the
      first two for you).
- [ ] If tenants can create the resource without bound, it calls `organizations.quotas`.

## Anything that reaches the network

- [ ] A URL somebody else chose goes through `apps.common.netguard` (https only, public addresses
      only, pinned IP, no redirects, bounded time and size).
- [ ] A fixed provider URL still verifies TLS. Never `verify=False`.
- [ ] Credentials come from settings, not code; secrets are never logged.

## A new setting or secret

- [ ] `env_*` helper with a comment above it (it becomes the reference docs).
- [ ] If production must constrain it, add a validator in `config/settings/validators.py` and a
      test; a missing or weak value must stop the boot with a message that names the variable.
- [ ] Added to `deploy/compose/prod.env.example` and the Kubernetes `configmap`/`secret` examples.

## A new page or template

- [ ] No inline script or style and no third-party origin (CSP is `'self'`).
- [ ] Forms are CSRF-protected; destructive links are POST.
- [ ] Copy is a label or a verb, not a paragraph that explains the screen.

## Logging, audit and errors

- [ ] Audit metadata: snake_case keys, ids and counts, no personal values (validated at write).
- [ ] No request bodies, tokens or addresses in logs (redaction is the net, not the plan).
- [ ] Internal errors reach the client as `server_error` plus `request_id`, nothing more.

## Background work

- [ ] Workflows import no Django; the work is an action called through `call_action`.
- [ ] A cron-style job is `@job` with a schedule; it is idempotent.
- [ ] A new webhook event is `register_event` and its payload carries ids only.

## Before you push

- [ ] `python scripts/verify.py` (full) is green.
- [ ] Generated files fresh: `actions_catalog`, `check_openapi.py --write`, `gen_docs.py`.
- [ ] Docs updated in `docs/en` **and** `docs/pt-BR`; `CHANGELOG.md` for anything a user sees.
- [ ] Nothing weakened to make a test pass (validators, CORS, `NETGUARD_ALLOW_PRIVATE`, `DEBUG`).
- [ ] For anything about the ANPD, children, or international transfers: a person with legal
      standing has looked at it.

<!-- docs/en/security/hardening.md -->

# Hardening and key management

## Production refuses to start when

- the secret key, the privacy HMAC key or the audit HMAC key is a placeholder, short or low-entropy,
  or two secrets are equal; a `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` / `PRIVACY_HMAC_KEYS_PREVIOUS` entry is weak;
- the field-encryption key ring is malformed or lacks the active key;
- the database is not reached over TLS **with certificate checking** (`sslmode=verify-ca` or
  `verify-full`); `require` encrypts without checking who answered and needs the explicit
  `DB_ALLOW_UNVERIFIED_TLS`, an unencrypted link needs `DB_ALLOW_INSECURE_TRANSPORT`;
- Redis is not `rediss://` (a password over plaintext protects nothing against a listener) unless
  `REDIS_ALLOW_INSECURE` records the decision;
- hosts are wildcard or origins are not https; `PUBLIC_URL` is not an https origin; no proxy is
  declared (`TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS`, `TRUSTED_PROXY_COUNT` or `TRUSTED_PROXY_DIRECT`); a proxy entry is
  not a CIDR;
- Temporal is on without sealed payloads, or without TLS / an API key / `TEMPORAL_ALLOW_INSECURE`;
- no controller or DPO channel is declared (`PRIVACY_CONTROLLER_NAME`, `DPO_EMAIL` or
  `DPO_CONTACT_URL`);
- the admin is enabled without `ADMIN_ALLOWED_IPS`; `NETGUARD_ALLOW_PRIVATE` is on; `LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG`.

`python scripts/verify.py` runs `manage.py check --deploy --fail-level WARNING` with production
settings: a warning is a failure. The two HSTS opt-ins (subdomains, preload) are silenced until you
turn them on because they are commitments about the whole parent domain.

## Always on

HTTPS redirect (health probes exempt), HSTS, secure/HTTP-only/SameSite cookies, a `'self'`-only CSP
with a violation sink, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` and
`Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy` `same-origin`, `Permissions-Policy` (camera, microphone, location,
payment ... off), `nosniff`, a strict referrer policy, no-store on API responses, an ASGI body-size
limit and body-read timeout (408), trusted-proxy client-IP resolution, Argon2 password hashing,
12-character password minimum with common-password check, CORS limited to `/api/`.

## Account protection

Staff need an authenticator for the admin; owners and administrators for the organization endpoints
(production); creating or rotating an API key needs a recent sign-in; a password or second-factor
reset revokes the person's keys; non-superuser staff cannot touch superusers; OAuth tokens are
stored as checksums. See [accounts](../guides/auth.md).

## Outbound requests

Everything a user can point the server at (webhooks, OAuth client metadata) passes the network
guard: `https` only, **global** addresses only (an allow-list: carrier-grade NAT, the Alibaba and
cloud metadata addresses, IPv6 tunnel forms and NAT64 wrappers of private IPv4 are refused), the
validated address is the one connected to, no redirects, no proxy from the environment, a total
deadline, a size cap, and no decompression. The Kubernetes NetworkPolicy repeats this at the network
layer: egress to the public internet excludes every private range and the metadata endpoint.

## Database roles

The runtime connects as a role that owns nothing; migrations run as the owner. See
[Deploy](../deploy/overview.md#two-database-identities) and [Audit integrity](audit-integrity.md).

## Key rotation

```bash
python scripts/generate_production_secrets.py --key-id v2 --existing-ring '{"v1":"..."}'
# set FIELD_ENCRYPTION_ACTIVE_KEY_ID=v2 and the new ring, deploy
python manage.py reencrypt_fields          # re-encrypts every encrypted column and the MFA secrets
# after it reports zero unreadable rows, remove v1 from the ring
```

Never regenerate the ring without `--existing-ring`: existing ciphertext would be unreadable.

| Secret | Rotation |
|---|---|
| `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY` | Old value to `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS`; nobody is logged out; drop it after the session lifetime |
| `PRIVACY_HMAC_KEY` | Old value to `PRIVACY_HMAC_KEYS_PREVIOUS`; API keys and data subjects are rewritten under the new key on first use |
| `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` | Starts a new epoch (older rows no longer verify under the new key): export the chain first |

## Rotating other credentials

API keys: `rotate` (24 h overlap). Webhook secrets: `rotate-secret` (both signatures sent during
overlap). OAuth clients: revoke tokens, issue a new client. Database/Redis passwords: rotate in
the platform, update the secret, roll the pods; `readiness` goes unready until connected.

## What this does not cover

A compromised host or build pipeline; a malicious superuser who also holds the keys (mitigated by
audit and the admin allow-list, not prevented); SSO/SCIM. See the [threat model](threat-model.md).

<!-- docs/en/security/review.md -->

# Security review

Status of the review of this template. Update this page whenever you change authentication,
tenancy, cryptography, logging or the outbound client.

## Baseline (start of the program): 36 findings

Two high severity (client IP collapsing behind a proxy, so throttles and lockouts were shared;
consent withdrawal could be blocked), the rest medium and low. All were fixed with a named
regression test in `tests/test_security_regressions.py`.

## Second review (2026-10)

A static review of settings, accounts, tenancy, audit, webhooks, flows, deployment and CI. Every
finding below was fixed with a named test unless noted.

| Severity | Finding | Resolution | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| High | The `uploads` app was untracked: an unanchored `.gitignore` rule hid it, so a clean clone could not start | Rules anchored; CI fails on ignored files under `src/` | CI step; `test_scaffold` copies the tree |
| High | Audit trail: any session could delete after setting a GUC; the hash was unkeyed; newest rows unverifiable; forged inserts outside the chain | Keyed HMAC chain, owner-only `audit_prune()`, role separation, `CHECK`, head export | `test_audit_integrity`, `test_the_chain_is_keyed...`, role-separation test (PostgreSQL) |
| Medium | SSRF guard missed carrier-grade NAT (100.64/10, Alibaba metadata), NAT64/6to4/Teredo wrappers; proxy from the environment; no total deadline; decompression | Allow-list of global addresses, embedded-IPv4 check, `trust_env=False`, deadline, raw bytes only | `test_netguard` |
| Medium | Staff with `change_user` could take over a superuser (edit the e-mail, reset) | Superusers hidden, e-mail read-only, password view superuser-only | `test_hardening` |
| Medium | No MFA for staff or owners; no recent sign-in to mint a key; keys survived a reset | `STAFF_MFA_REQUIRED`, `ORG_PRIVILEGED_MFA_REQUIRED`, recent-auth window, revoke on reset | `test_hardening` |
| Medium | OAuth tokens stored in clear; no refresh-replay protection; DCR accepted `client_credentials`, `http` redirects and never expired | RFC 9700 gates on, checksum storage, reuse protection, registration policy and expiry, `iss` | `test_hardening`, `test_oauth`, `test_mcp_protocol` |
| Medium | Temporal accepted unsealed payloads (forgeable activity input); `run_task` imported any dotted path; no boot validation | Unsealed refused, task bridge restricted, validators | `test_flows`, `test_hardening` |
| Medium | Key rotation missed MFA seeds; MFA decrypt accepted plaintext; HMAC rotation broke every key | `reencrypt_fields` covers MFA, plaintext refused, `PRIVACY_HMAC_KEYS_PREVIOUS`, `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` | `test_key_rotation` |
| Medium | Export link reusable for 7 days, relative in the mail, token in the URL path of logs | Download cap, absolute `PUBLIC_URL`, token scrubbed | `test_export_link` |
| Medium | Failed-login and refused-action audit rows were attacker-controlled in volume; per-id key lockout let a stranger lock out the owner | Per-client ceilings, per-address failure counters | `test_abuse_limits` |
| Medium | Deployment: open egress, one superuser database identity for everything, `:latest`, unencrypted backups, no release gate | NetworkPolicy ipBlock, two roles, digests, umask and TLS on backups, release gated on CI with signing | CI (render, trivy config, boot) |
| Low | No Permissions-Policy / CORP; CORS covered every path; no CSP sink; admin path without slash leaked; html 500s for the API; objects bypassed log redaction; legacy login | Added, scoped, or switched off | `test_web_hardening` |
| Low | Tenant isolation was convention only; undo looked up the target by id alone; unbounded per-tenant resources | Structural tests, organization filter in undo, quotas | `test_tenancy_structure` |
| Low | Database TLS `require` and Redis password-only accepted; slow request bodies; deploy check passed on warnings | Verified TLS, `rediss`, 408 on stalled bodies, warnings fail | `test_security_regressions`, `test_body_timeout` |

## Open items

| Item | Notes |
|---|---|
| Row-level security | A documented option, not implemented ([ADR 14](../adr/row-level-security.md)) |
| Breached-password check | Not built: it needs an outbound call to a third party; add it as an allauth password validator through `netguard` if you want it |
| Idle session timeout | Sessions have an absolute lifetime (`SESSION_COOKIE_AGE_SECONDS`, 12 h); add a sliding idle limit if your threat model asks |
| Per-user authorization for flows | A flow runs as the person who started it with that person's role, but not with the starting credential's scopes: declare each flow's scope to cover everything it does |
| Image base digests | The application image is signed and deployed by digest; pin the base image by digest in your registry mirror for byte-for-byte rebuilds |
| Per-user AAD for MFA secrets | allauth's adapter hook passes no user, so seeds are bound to the column, not the person |
| `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` rotation | New epoch, no tooling yet ([ADR 13](../adr/audit-chain-and-role-split.md)) |

Report vulnerabilities as described in `SECURITY.md`.

<!-- docs/en/security/threat-model.md -->

# Threat model

| Asset | Threat | Control |
|---|---|---|
| Another organization's data | IDOR, missing tenant filter, writable foreign key to a foreign row | Single ORM door in actions (`ctx.scoped`, AST test over `actions.py`, `actions/*.py`, `agent.py`), `OrganizationScopedViewSet`, `OrgScopedPrimaryKeyRelatedField`, every organization column scoped or explained (test), undo filters by organization, role checked per call; row-level security is a documented option ([ADR 14](../adr/row-level-security.md)) |
| Shared capacity | One tenant fills the database, the bucket or the key table | Per-organization quotas (`QUOTA_*`) |
| Credentials | Brute force, stuffing, enumeration | Argon2, axes lockout on every sign-in path (IPv6 /64 buckets), allauth rate limits, uniform responses, MFA |
| Privileged accounts | Staff-to-superuser takeover; admin with a password alone | Superusers hidden from other staff, e-mail and password views superuser-only, MFA required for the admin and (production) for owners and administrators |
| API keys | Theft, over-privilege, key-mints-key, survival of a takeover | Keyed blind-index storage, scopes default-deny, validated IP allow-list, expiry, session-only creation with a recent sign-in, 24 h rotation overlap, revoked on password / MFA reset, failures counted per key+address |
| Tokens (OAuth) | Replay at another service; database dump | PKCE `S256`, audience binding (RFC 8707), stored as checksum, rotating refresh with family revocation, RFC 9207 `iss`, https/loopback redirects only, throttled and policy-checked registration |
| Secrets in the database | Dump or backup leak | AES-GCM field encryption with key ring and rotation (`reencrypt_fields`, MFA seeds included), encrypted idempotency responses and undo snapshots, tokens as checksums |
| Logs and traces | PII leakage | Redaction at the end of the pipeline (including objects rendered with `str`), secret URL paths scrubbed, golden-log test, Temporal payload encryption |
| Outbound calls | SSRF, DNS rebinding, tunnelled private addresses | `netguard`: https, global addresses only, pinned IP, no redirects, no env proxy, deadline, no decompression; NetworkPolicy egress excludes private ranges |
| Data subject export | A mailed link that outlives its purpose | Sealed archive, expiring link capped at `PRIVACY_EXPORT_MAX_DOWNLOADS`, token scrubbed from logs, absolute `PUBLIC_URL` |
| Uploads | Malware, polyglots, zip bombs, stored XSS, orphaned files | Content sniffing, extension rules, zip limits, attachment + nosniff + CSP sandbox, optional ClamAV, file removed with its row on every path |
| Audit trail | Tampering by a compromised app account or by a database writer | Keyed hash chain per organization, owner-only prune function, runtime role with `INSERT`/`SELECT` only, `CHECK` against rows outside the chain, `audit_verify` and head export ([ADR 13](../adr/audit-chain-and-role-split.md)) |
| Workflow engine | A stranger on the Temporal network starts an activity as anyone | Sealed payloads required (an unsealed one is refused), TLS or API key validated at boot, `run_task` limited to declared tasks under allowed prefixes |
| Availability | Large or slow bodies, floods | ASGI body cap and read timeout, per-IP and per-credential budgets, bounded responses |
| Supply chain | Vulnerable or malicious dependency, tampered image | Locked deps, weekly `pip-audit` of `uv.lock`, Dependabot, SBOM, pinned Actions and images, Trivy, CodeQL, zizmor, release gated on CI, cosign signature, provenance, deploy by digest |
| Agents (MCP) | Prompt-injected destructive actions | Scopes, role, `destructive` hints, an explicit undo decision per write action, undo journal, run ledger, text in records treated as data, behaviour prompt |
| The codebase itself | A change (human or AI) that removes a control | Rules enforced by tests, conformance suite over every action, generated agent files kept fresh, `check_conventions` |

Out of scope: a compromised host or build pipeline, malicious superusers who also hold the keys
(mitigated by audit and the admin allow-list, not prevented), SSO/SCIM, denial of service at the
network layer.

<!-- docs/en/lgpd/compliance-matrix.md -->

# LGPD compliance matrix

Article → platform feature → code → test. "Operator" means the organization running the system
must still do something. Interpretations are marked **to validate**.

| Art. | Requirement | Platform | Code | Test |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5, 39, 42 | Controller and operator | Guidance, DPA template; data model not split by role ([ADR 17](../adr/controller-and-operator.md)); operator: decide and write it down | - | - |
| 6 | Principles (purpose, necessity, security) | Purposes with retention; classification forces a decision per model | `privacy.models.ProcessingPurpose`, `privacy.catalog` | `test_every_model_has_been_classified`, `test_catalog_lint` |
| 7-8 | Lawful basis; consent | Basis per purpose; consent records with frozen notice digest, keyed chain; visitor cookie choices | `privacy.models.ConsentRecord`, `CookieConsent` | `test_lgpd`, `test_lgpd_extras` |
| 8 par. 2 | Proof of consent | Keyed hash chain, evidence hashes | `common.encryption.chain_digest` | `test_lgpd` |
| 9 | Access to information on processing | Public notice, purposes (with the consequence of refusing), sub-processors | `privacy.public_api` | `test_lgpd`, `test_lgpd_extras` |
| 11 | Sensitive data | Category `sensitive`; encrypted fields enforced by test; **restricting the allowed bases is operator work (to validate)** | `privacy.catalog.Category`, `common.encryption` | `test_catalog_lint` |
| 12 | Anonymized data | Anonymization executors; pseudonymised audit rows are kept: **whether they are personal data is to validate** | `privacy.services` | `test_lgpd` |
| 14 | Children | Category `child` (encrypted), guardian confirmation, age-assurance seam, ECA Digital notes; operator chooses the method | `privacy.age`, `ProcessingPurpose.involves_children` | `test_lgpd_extras` |
| 15-16 | End of processing; retention | Sweep with dry run; dormant accounts, uploads, keys, cookie consents; legal holds | `privacy.retention` | `test_lgpd`, `test_lgpd_retention` |
| 18 I | Confirmation | Answer says whether data is held | `privacy.services` | `test_lgpd_extras` |
| 18 II, V | Access; portability | Sealed export, limited-use link; **ANPD format still pending** (to validate) | `privacy.services` | `test_export_link` |
| 18 III | Correction | Routed to a person (`legal_review`) | `privacy.services` | `test_lgpd` |
| 18 IV, VI | Anonymization, blocking, deletion | Executors from the catalog; stored files removed; step-up by mail | `privacy.services`, `uploads.signals` | `test_lgpd`, `test_lgpd_retention` |
| 18 VII | Who data is shared with | Active sub-processors; stubs for the platform's own vendors | `privacy.public_api`, `privacy_seed` | `test_lgpd_extras` |
| 18 VIII | Consequence of refusing consent | `ProcessingPurpose.refusal_consequence`, published with the purpose | `privacy.public_api` | `test_lgpd_extras` |
| 18 IX | Withdrawal | Always possible, never throttled | `privacy.services` | `test_lgpd` |
| 19 | Response deadlines | Target days setting; reminders; overdue | `privacy.deadlines`, `privacy.jobs` | `test_lgpd` |
| 33 | International transfer | `SubProcessor.transfer_mechanism`, country; **clause texts and the ANPD standard clauses are operator work (Res. CD/ANPD 19/2024)** | `privacy.models.SubProcessor` | `test_lgpd_extras` |
| 37 | Record of processing | RoPA export from the catalog (**table level: recipients and security measures are operator text**) | `manage.py privacy_ropa` | `test_lgpd` |
| 38 | Impact report (RIPD) | `ImpactAssessment` model and template | `privacy.models.ImpactAssessment` | `test_lgpd_extras` |
| 41 | DPO | `DPO_*` published and required in production; contact endpoint | `privacy.public_api`, `settings.validators` | `test_lgpd_extras` |
| 46-47 | Security | Hardening, MFA, encryption, keyed audit, strict production validators | see [hardening](../security/hardening.md) | `test_security_regressions`, `test_hardening` |
| 48 | Incident communication | Incident model; ANPD and subjects deadlines, 20-business-day complement, small-agent doubling, content export (**clock start and 3 business days: to validate**) | `privacy.models.PersonalDataIncident`, `privacy_incident_export` | `test_lgpd`, `test_lgpd_extras` |
| 50 | Governance | Keyed audit chain, runbooks | `audit`, [runbooks](../deploy/runbooks.md) | `test_audit_integrity` |
| ECA Digital | Age assurance, privacy by default (Lei 15.211/2025) | The seam above; **applicability is a legal question** | `privacy.age` | `test_lgpd_extras` |

Not covered by software: choosing legal bases, writing notices (templates help), international
transfer clauses, RIPD content, training, contracts with processors, the controller/operator
split. The platform gives you the register, the evidence and the executors; people decide.


---

<!-- docs/en/lgpd/overview.md -->

# LGPD (Brazilian data protection) overview

> Engineering documentation, not legal advice. Deadlines, legal bases and the content of notices
> are settings and data you must confirm with your DPO or counsel. Items marked **to validate**
> are interpretations, not facts.

## What is built in

| Duty | Where |
|---|---|
| Know what you hold (art. 37, RoPA) | `<app>/privacy.py` classifies **every** model; a test fails until you do, another when a personal-looking field is not listed. `manage.py privacy_ropa` exports the register of processing; [catalog](../reference/data-catalog.md) |
| Purposes and lawful bases (arts. 6-7) | `ProcessingPurpose` with lawful basis, data categories, retention days and the consequence of refusing; seeded by `manage.py privacy_seed` |
| Consent (art. 8) | `ConsentRecord`: HMAC-chained per person, frozen notice and purpose digests, evidence (IP hash, UA hash). **Withdrawal is always possible** and is never rate limited. Cookie choices of visitors without an account are recorded as proof (`POST /api/v1/privacy/cookies/consent/`) |
| Transparency (arts. 9, 41) | Public endpoints: active notice, controller and DPO (`DPO_*`, `PRIVACY_CONTROLLER_*`, **required in production**), purposes, sub-processors and transfers, cookie categories. Texts in Portuguese by default (`PRIVACY_MAIL_LANGUAGE`) |
| Data subject rights (art. 18) | `DataSubjectRequest` for the 11 request types, intake for people without an account (e-mail verification), state machine with guarded transitions, SLA reminders; confirmation says whether data is held |
| Erasure, anonymization, blocking, export | Executors driven by the catalog; export is a sealed package behind an expiring, limited-use link; stored files leave the bucket with their rows |
| Retention (arts. 15-16) | `manage.py retention_sweep [--dry-run]` covers models with a `retention_field`, including uploads, API keys, cookie consents and **dormant accounts** (anonymized after the purpose's retention without sign-in; staff and people under a legal hold are never swept) |
| Incidents (art. 48) | `PersonalDataIncident`: ANPD deadline in business days (`PRIVACY_INCIDENT_BUSINESS_DAYS`, `PRIVACY_HOLIDAYS`, doubled by `PRIVACY_SMALL_AGENT`), the same period for the people affected, a 20-business-day window to complete a communication, reminders, `privacy_incident_export` |
| Impact assessment (art. 38) | `ImpactAssessment` model and a [template](templates.md) |
| Security (art. 46) | See [hardening](../security/hardening.md): encryption at rest for sensitive fields, keyed audit chain, MFA, strict production validators |
| Children (art. 14) and the ECA Digital | See below |
| Sub-processors and transfers (art. 33) | `SubProcessor` with country and transfer mechanism; `privacy_seed` creates **inactive** stubs for the platform's own vendors (Sentry, object storage, mail, Temporal, hosting) that you activate and complete |

## Children and the ECA Digital

LGPD art. 14 requires a parent's or guardian's specific consent for a child's data. The ECA Digital
(Lei 15.211/2025, in force since 17 March 2026; a regulating decree followed, as reported: check the primary text) goes further for
products likely to be used by minors: reliable, auditable age assurance (self-declaration does not
qualify), privacy by design and by default, and an impact assessment. **Whether it applies to your
product, and which method is adequate, is a legal question, and the ANPD's guidance is still
developing: confirm with counsel.**

What the platform gives you: the `child` data category (fields must be encrypted), purposes that
`involves_children` and demand `guardian_confirmed` on consent, and a seam for age assurance:
`AGE_ASSURANCE_BACKEND` names a class with `assess(user) -> AgeAssurance`
(`apps/privacy/age.py`). A consent grant from a person the backend reports as a minor is refused
without guardian confirmation. The default backend admits it cannot tell and changes nothing; a
product aimed at minors must replace it. Keep the decision (`is_minor`, how it was reached), never
the document.

## Requests

`access`, `confirmation`, `correction`, `anonymization`, `blocking`, `deletion`, `portability`,
`consent_withdrawal`, `sharing_information`, `automated_review`, `opposition`.

Status path: `received → verifying → in_progress → (legal_review) → completed | denied | cancelled`.
No other transition exists; illegal ones raise. The target response time is
`PRIVACY_REQUEST_TARGET_DAYS` (15) - **to validate** against the regulation in force. Correction,
opposition and automated-decision review go to `legal_review`: a person decides. **Destructive**
types (deletion, anonymization, blocking) require the requester to confirm by a mailed link before
anything is executed.

## Who is the controller

For your customers' account and billing data you are the controller; for what their members put
in the product you are usually the operator and the customer the controller. See
[ADR 17](../adr/controller-and-operator.md) and the
[data processing agreement template](templates.md): settle this with counsel before the first
customer.

## Running it

DSAR processing is a flow (Temporal workflow, or the local engine), with reminders at D-5 and
D-1 and an overdue state. Jobs: `privacy.dsar_sweep`, `privacy.dsar_sla`,
`privacy.incident_deadlines`, `privacy.retention_sweep`, `privacy.exports_cleanup`.

## Setup checklist

1. Set `PRIVACY_CONTROLLER_NAME`, `PRIVACY_CONTROLLER_ID` (CNPJ), `DPO_NAME`, `DPO_EMAIL`,
   `DPO_CONTACT_URL` (production refuses to start without a controller and a DPO channel).
2. `python manage.py privacy_seed` and review each purpose (basis, retention, consequence of
   refusing) with counsel; activate the sub-processors you use.
3. Publish a `PrivacyNotice` (immutable once active; publish a new version to change it) built from
   the [templates](templates.md).
4. List holidays in `PRIVACY_HOLIDAYS` for the deadline arithmetic.
5. Register your own models in `<app>/privacy.py` and rerun `scripts/gen_docs.py`.
6. `python manage.py doctor` reports what is still missing; review the
   [compliance matrix](compliance-matrix.md) for what the platform does not cover.

<!-- docs/en/lgpd/templates.md -->

# LGPD document templates

Starting points for the documents the LGPD asks you to have. **They are templates, not legal
advice.** The text depends on your processing, your contracts and your sector; have a lawyer with
LGPD experience adapt and approve each one before it is published or signed. Placeholders are
`{{like this}}`.

| Document | Template | Used with |
|---|---|---|
| Privacy notice (arts. 6, 9, 18) | [English](../../templates/privacy-policy.en.md) - [Português](../../templates/privacy-policy.pt-BR.md) | `PrivacyNotice`; the public transparency endpoint |
| Terms of service | [English](../../templates/terms-of-service.en.md) - [Português](../../templates/terms-of-service.pt-BR.md) | Sign-up flow |
| Data processing agreement (arts. 5, 39, 42) | [English](../../templates/data-processing-agreement.en.md) - [Português](../../templates/data-processing-agreement.pt-BR.md) | Customers for whom you are the operator |
| Impact assessment, RIPD (art. 38) | [English](../../templates/dpia-ripd.en.md) - [Português](../../templates/dpia-ripd.pt-BR.md) | `ImpactAssessment` model |

## Filling them from the platform

- **Controller and DPO**: `PRIVACY_CONTROLLER_NAME`, `PRIVACY_CONTROLLER_ID`, `DPO_NAME`,
  `DPO_EMAIL`, `DPO_CONTACT_URL` (also published by `GET /api/v1/privacy/transparency/`).
- **What you collect and why**: `python manage.py privacy_ropa` prints the register generated from
  the data catalog; the purposes, lawful bases and retention come from `ProcessingPurpose`.
- **Who else sees the data**: the active `SubProcessor` rows (name, country, transfer mechanism).
- **How long you keep it**: each purpose's `retention_days`, plus `AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS`.
- **Rights and how to use them**: the public request endpoint and the 15-day response target.
- **Cookies**: the categories at `GET /api/v1/privacy/cookies/` and the consent record you keep.

## Publishing the notice

A published `PrivacyNotice` is immutable (consents point at its checksum). Put the document at a
stable URL, compute the SHA-256 of **the document**, create the notice with both, and activate it.
To change it, publish a new version.

## Review rhythm

Re-read the notice and the register when you add a purpose, a sub-processor, a country or a
category of data; at least once a year otherwise.

<!-- docs/en/deploy/overview.md -->

# Deploy anywhere

One container image, several roles chosen by the first argument:

| Role | Command | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `web` (default) | `entrypoint web` | gunicorn + uvicorn workers on `$PORT` |
| `worker` | `entrypoint worker` | Temporal worker (only with `TEMPORAL_ENABLED=true`) |
| `scheduler` | `entrypoint scheduler` | cron-style jobs when Temporal is off; exactly one replica |
| `migrate` | `entrypoint migrate` | `migrate` (+ `flows_sync` with Temporal), then exit |
| `job NAME` | `entrypoint job maintenance.prune_audit` | one job, for cron/CronJob |
| `manage ...` | `entrypoint manage doctor` | any management command |

`DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=config.settings.production` is baked in. The minimum environment is in
[Troubleshooting](../guides/troubleshooting.md); the strict validators name what is missing, and
[env vars](../reference/env-vars.md) lists everything. The image runs as a non-root user and works
with a read-only root filesystem (`/tmp` writable). Build with
`--build-arg EXTRAS="--extra otel"` if you want OpenTelemetry in the image.

## Targets

| Where | How |
|---|---|
| Single host | `deploy/compose/compose.prod.yaml`: Caddy (automatic TLS), migrate, web, scheduler, Postgres, Redis, optional `--profile temporal` (server, UI, schema job) and `--profile backup` |
| Kubernetes | `deploy/k8s/base` + `overlays/production` (kustomize): restricted pod security, probes, HPA, PDB, default-deny NetworkPolicy with public-internet-only egress, backup CronJob; run `migrate-job.yaml` before each rollout |
| PaaS (Heroku-style, Dokku, Coolify, Railway, Render) | `Procfile` (release/web/worker/scheduler); provide Postgres and optionally Redis |
| Cloud Run, ECS, Nomad, any other PaaS | Run the same image; map `web` to the service and `migrate` to the release/pre-deploy step |
| Bare metal / VM | Install the wheel set from `requirements.txt`, run gunicorn under systemd behind nginx/Caddy; `scheduler` as a second unit |

## Two database identities

The schema owner runs migrations; the application connects as a role that owns nothing. That
separation is what makes the audit trail resistant to a compromised web process
([ADR 13](../adr/audit-chain-and-role-split.md)).

- Compose: `DB_USER` (owner) is used by `migrate` and Temporal only; web, scheduler and worker use
  `APP_DB_USER` / `APP_DB_PASSWORD`. The role is created on first start by
  `deploy/compose/initdb/10-runtime-role.sh`.
- Kubernetes: `app-secrets` holds the runtime role (`DB_USER`/`DB_PASSWORD`); the `migrate` Job reads
  the owner from the `app-migrator` secret and receives `AUDIT_RUNTIME_ROLE`.
- Elsewhere: create the role yourself, grant it `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE` on tables and
  `USAGE, SELECT` on sequences (default privileges for what the owner creates later), and set
  `AUDIT_RUNTIME_ROLE` to its name when you run `migrate`.

`manage.py doctor` reports when the runtime role can still rewrite the trail.

## Checklist

1. Generate secrets: `python scripts/generate_production_secrets.py`.
2. Declare the proxy (`TRUSTED_PROXY_COUNT=1` behind one load balancer, or CIDRs) and `PUBLIC_URL`.
3. Postgres with verified TLS (`sslmode=verify-full`), Redis over `rediss://`; on a private network
   you control, the explicit `DB_ALLOW_INSECURE_TRANSPORT` / `REDIS_ALLOW_INSECURE` record that
   decision.
4. Run `migrate`, then roll `web`. Probes: liveness `/api/v1/health/live/`, readiness
   `/api/v1/health/ready/` (both exempt from the HTTPS redirect).
5. `entrypoint manage doctor --strict` in the pipeline.
6. Uploads and exports: set `S3_BUCKET`, or mount a volume at `/app/media` with
   `OBJECT_STORAGE_REQUIRED=false`.
7. Set the controller and DPO (`PRIVACY_CONTROLLER_NAME`, `DPO_EMAIL`): production refuses to start
   without them.
8. Schedule backups ([runbooks](runbooks.md)); store them encrypted.
9. Ship the audit head lines (`audit_head` log events) to a system the database cannot reach.

## Releasing

Tag `vX.Y.Z`. The release workflow runs the full CI gate, builds the image, scans it (Trivy), signs it
(cosign, keyless), attaches provenance and an SBOM as OCI attestations and creates a GitHub
Release naming the image **digest**. Deploy by digest (`image@sha256:...`), in the Kubernetes
overlay and the migrate Job alike: a tag can be moved, a digest cannot. CI also renders the Compose
file and the kustomize overlay, scans the manifests for misconfiguration and boots the built image
with production settings.


---

<!-- docs/en/deploy/runbooks.md -->

# Runbooks

## Backup and restore

- Logical backup: compose `--profile backup` or the Kubernetes CronJob writes
  `pg_dump --format=custom` nightly (owner-only file mode) and keeps 14 days. Dumps hold **every
  tenant's data in the clear**: keep the volume encrypted and copy dumps off the machine encrypted.
- Restore into an empty database: `pg_restore --clean --if-exists --no-owner -d "$DB" file.dump`,
  then `entrypoint migrate` (as the schema owner, with `AUDIT_RUNTIME_ROLE` set), then
  `entrypoint manage audit_verify`.
- **Re-apply erasures after a restore.** A restore brings back people who were erased after the
  backup was taken, and the platform keeps no identity after an erasure. Keep a ledger **outside
  the database** (request id, date, and how to identify the person, under access control) of
  erasures made since the last backup, and repeat each one after a restore. Short backup retention
  shrinks the problem; say the retention in the privacy notice.
- Keep the **encryption key ring** and `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` with the backups' recovery material, stored
  apart from them: without the ring encrypted columns are unreadable; without the audit key the
  chain cannot be verified.
- Practise a restore at least quarterly; the goal is a timed, written procedure.

## Personal data incident

1. Create the incident (admin or API): discovery time, categories, estimated subjects, measures.
2. The ANPD notice deadline is computed in business days (`PRIVACY_INCIDENT_BUSINESS_DAYS`,
   `PRIVACY_HOLIDAYS`, doubled by `PRIVACY_SMALL_AGENT`); the people affected have the same
   period; a first communication may be completed up to 20 business days after it. Reminders fire
   hourly via `privacy.incident_deadlines`.
3. Contain: revoke API keys and OAuth tokens, rotate secrets ([hardening](../security/hardening.md)),
   disable affected webhook endpoints.
4. Preserve evidence: `audit_verify`, export audit rows for the window.
5. Decide notification of the ANPD and the people affected with the DPO and counsel
   (**the clock starting at confirmation, 3 business days and who counts as a small agent are to
   validate**), assemble the content with `manage.py privacy_incident_export REF`, then record the
   outcome and close. Records are kept five years.

## Audit chain broken

`audit_verify` exits non-zero (or the daily job logs `audit_chain_broken`): stop pruning, snapshot
the database, find the first bad row, compare with the latest backup, treat as a security incident.
`newest events are missing` means the chain was cut at the end: compare with the head lines you
shipped. Also run `manage.py doctor`: if the runtime role can rewrite the trail, fix that first.

## Rotating secrets

| Secret | Procedure |
|---|---|
| `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY` | Move the old value to `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS`, set the new one, deploy; drop the old after `SESSION_COOKIE_AGE_SECONDS` |
| Field-encryption key | New id in the ring, switch the active id, `manage.py reencrypt_fields` (also reseals MFA secrets), drop the old key after it reports zero unreadable |
| `PRIVACY_HMAC_KEY` | Put the old value in `PRIVACY_HMAC_KEYS_PREVIOUS`, set the new one; API keys and data subjects are rewritten on first use; drop the old once keys have been used or reissued |
| `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` | Not rotatable in place: start a new epoch (export the old chain, then new key) |
| Database / Redis password | Rotate in the platform, update the secret, roll the pods; `readiness` goes unready until connected |
| API keys, webhook secrets | `rotate` / `rotate-secret` (24 h overlap) |
| OAuth clients | Revoke tokens, issue a new client |

## Temporal unavailable

`/api/v1/health/ready/` stays up (worker state is informational). Starts of Temporal-only flows
fail fast; portable flows keep working only if you set `TEMPORAL_ENABLED=false` and run the
`scheduler`. After recovery run `flows_sync`. Webhook deliveries retry on their own.

## A webhook endpoint is disabled

It reached `WEBHOOK_DISABLE_AFTER` consecutive failures. Fix the receiver, re-enable the endpoint,
then `redeliver` the failed deliveries.

## Upgrade

Read `CHANGELOG.md`; deploy order: migrate job, then web, then worker/scheduler. Migrations are
additive between minor releases. Roll back the image, not the database. See
[Upgrading from upstream](../guides/upgrading.md).


---

<!-- docs/en/migration/from-celery.md -->

# Upgrading from the Celery-era template

Applies to projects copied from earlier versions of this template. Move one project at a time;
keep the others on their tag until you do.

1. **Dependencies**: Django 6.1.2, DRF 3.18.x; remove `celery`; add the new requirements.
2. **Settings**: replace `CELERY_*` with `TEMPORAL_*` (see [env vars](../reference/env-vars.md));
   platform-specific variables from the old template are gone. Declare your proxy: `TRUSTED_PROXY_COUNT` or `TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS`.
   New required production variables: `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY`, `PUBLIC_URL`, `PRIVACY_CONTROLLER_NAME`,
   `DPO_EMAIL`/`DPO_CONTACT_URL` ([troubleshooting](../guides/troubleshooting.md)).
3. **Tasks**: `@shared_task` functions become `@job` (scheduled/manual) or `django.tasks` tasks;
   `.delay()` becomes `task.enqueue()`; beat schedules become the `schedule=` of the job.
4. **Workers**: run `entrypoint worker` (Temporal) or `entrypoint scheduler` (no Temporal).
5. **Migrations**: new apps (`actions`, `apikeys`, `flows`, `webhooks`, `flags`, `uploads`,
   allauth, usersessions) are additive. Run `migrate` **as the schema owner**, then
   `manage.py privacy_seed`.
6. **Models**: add `<app>/privacy.py` classifications; the test suite will list what is missing.
7. **Encryption**: values written by v1 keep decrypting; run `reencrypt_fields` once to move
   them to the v2 format.
8. **Accounts**: existing users get no verified address; with mandatory verification they
   verify on their next sign-in. To skip it for a trusted user base, create verified
   `EmailAddress` rows before cutover. `/api/v1/auth/login/` is off by default
   (`LEGACY_LOGIN_ENABLED`).
9. **Audit**: the chain is keyed from the start. Rows written by an older template used a plain
   hash and will not verify under the key: archive them, then start the chain fresh.
10. **Deploy**: switch to the new Dockerfile entrypoint roles or compose/k8s manifests, which also
    create the two database roles.


---

<!-- docs/en/adr/ai-context-generated.md -->

# ADR 16: Agent-facing files are generated from one rulebook

**Status:** accepted.

## Context

Agents read different files (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, Cursor rules, Copilot instructions,
`llms.txt`). Written by hand they drift from each other and from the code, and an agent that
follows a stale rule produces a wrong change with total confidence.

## Decision

`src/devtools/conventions.py` holds the rules as data: each with its reason and what enforces it.
`scripts/gen_docs.py` renders every agent-facing file from it and `--check` fails CI on drift.
Only rules that something enforces, or that are a human judgement said as such, are listed.
`docs/reference/conventions.json` carries the same rules plus what is registered right now (actions,
scopes, events, jobs, models), for programs.

## Consequences

- One edit changes every copy. The cost is one more generated file set to keep fresh, covered by the
  same `verify.py` gate as the OpenAPI and reference docs.
- A rule that nothing enforces is a promise; the rulebook is deliberately short for that reason.
- Languages: the agent files are English (what coding agents read best); the human guides exist in
  English and Portuguese.


---

<!-- docs/en/adr/audit-chain-and-role-split.md -->

# ADR 13: The audit trail is keyed, and only an owner can prune it

**Status:** accepted. Replaces the unkeyed chain described in decision 8.

## Context

The trail is hash-chained per organization and guarded by a PostgreSQL trigger. A review found
three ways that was weaker than the documentation claimed:

1. The hash was plain SHA-256, so anyone able to write the table could rewrite history and recompute
   every hash consistently.
2. The trigger allowed a `DELETE` after `SET LOCAL app.audit_maintenance = 'on'`, which *any*
   session can run, so a compromised application account could erase the trail.
3. A chain proves what *precedes* its head. Deleting the newest events leaves a shorter chain that
   still verifies.

## Decision

- **Keyed chain.** Each hash is an HMAC under `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` (environment, never the database).
  A database writer cannot re-chain without it. The same helper keys the consent chain.
- **Owner-only prune.** The trigger allows a delete only for the role that owns the table, and the
  only sanctioned delete is `audit_prune(chain, up_to_seq)`, a `SECURITY DEFINER` function whose
  `EXECUTE` is granted to the runtime role named in `AUDIT_RUNTIME_ROLE`. The runtime role has
  `INSERT` and `SELECT` on the table and nothing else (its `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE` are revoked
  by the migration). `doctor` warns when the runtime owns the table.
- **No row outside the chain.** A `CHECK (seq IS NOT NULL AND hash <> '')` refuses forged inserts
  (added `NOT VALID`, so rows from before chaining do not block it).
- **Heads leave the database.** The daily `maintenance.verify_audit` job logs each chain's head;
  `audit_verify --expect heads.json` compares a recorded head with the chain and catches tail
  removal.

## Consequences

- True only with two database roles (schema owner for migrations, runtime for the app). The Compose
  and Kubernetes manifests create them; a single-role deployment still gets the keyed chain, loses
  the privilege separation, and `doctor` says so.
- A superuser who also holds `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` can still rewrite history. Ship the head lines to a
  system the database cannot reach (a log service with write-once storage) to detect that too.
- Rotating `AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` invalidates verification of older rows: start a new epoch, export the
  old chain first. No tooling for that yet; it is a deliberate non-goal until a customer needs it.


---

<!-- docs/en/adr/controller-and-operator.md -->

# ADR 17: Who is the controller, and whose request is it

**Status:** accepted as guidance; the data model is **not** split by role yet.

## Context

LGPD distinguishes the **controller** (decides purposes and means) from the **operator** (processes
on the controller's behalf) (arts. 5, 37, 39, 42). In a multi-tenant product both appear:

- For its own customers' accounts, billing and security records, the **platform owner is the
  controller**.
- For the data a customer's members put into the product, the **customer organization is the
  controller** and the platform owner the **operator**.

The platform's `DataSubject` and `DataSubjectRequest` are global, not scoped to an organization:
one person, one record, one place to ask.

## Decision

- Document the split (this ADR, the offboarding guide, the data-processing-agreement template) and
  have the customer contract state it. Code does not decide it.
- Keep requests global for **platform-controller** data. For **operator** data, the platform owner
  forwards the request to the customer organization (the DPA fixes the time limit) and provides the
  executors (export, erase, block) the organization uses.
- Defer a per-organization privacy profile (controller name, DPO, notice URL per tenant) until a
  customer needs to publish its own: the transparency endpoint publishes the platform owner's.

## Consequences

- Erasure of a person reaches every organization they belong to, because the person is global. A
  product where one person can be a member of unrelated customers should decide, with counsel,
  whether a request from one customer's member may touch another customer's data. The default (it
  may not for operator data; it may for platform-controller data) needs a per-model flag in the
  catalog if you need that precision.
- This is the point most worth a lawyer's time before the first customer.


---

<!-- docs/en/adr/index.md -->

# Decisions

Short records of choices that shape the code. Each states the reason and the cost.

1. **Actions are the only way in.** One registry feeds REST, MCP, Temporal and the CLI. Cost: an
   extra layer for trivial CRUD, which `OrganizationScopedViewSet` still serves.
2. **pydantic is the single schema source** for actions (REST docs, MCP input schema, activity
   types). No parallel DRF serializers for actions.
3. **Celery removed.** Background work is `django.tasks` with a Temporal backend, or the
   immediate backend when Temporal is off. Cost: no Celery ecosystem.
4. **Temporal is optional, the local engine is honest.** Same `flows.start()`, with a published
   capability matrix; non-portable flows say so. Cost: two implementations to test.
5. **Sync activities on a thread pool.** Django's ORM is synchronous; connections are closed
   around each activity.
6. **Workflows import no Django.** The sandbox forbids it; activities do the work.
7. **Temporal payloads are encrypted** by a codec, arguments are ids, and an unsealed payload is
   refused.
8. **Audit chain per organization** with an advisory lock at insert, plus a trigger. Cost: write
   contention on very hot organizations; batch sealing is the escape hatch. Hardened by decision 13.
9. **Every model is classified for LGPD** by a failing test.
10. **allauth for accounts**, DOT for OAuth. Cost: two libraries; benefit: audited flows for MFA,
    verification and consent.
11. **Closed sign-up by default.** Open systems are an explicit choice.
12. **One image, many roles; no platform lock-in.** Any container platform is a target.

Longer records:

13. [The audit trail is keyed, and only an owner can prune it](audit-chain-and-role-split.md)
14. [Row-level security is an opt-in design, not the default](row-level-security.md)
15. [Two MCP servers, with different jobs](two-mcp-servers.md)
16. [Agent-facing files are generated from one rulebook](ai-context-generated.md)
17. [Who is the controller, and whose request is it](controller-and-operator.md)


---

<!-- docs/en/adr/row-level-security.md -->

# ADR 14: Row-level security is an opt-in design, not the default

**Status:** accepted as a documented option. **Not implemented.**

## Context

Tenant isolation today is by construction: actions read only through `ctx.scoped`/`ctx.get`, the
viewset base filters by organization, writable foreign keys are validated against the organization,
and tests scan the code and exercise cross-tenant access. That is convention, enforced by tests. A
bug that bypasses it (a raw query, a forgotten filter in code outside `actions.py`) leaks across
tenants. PostgreSQL row-level security (RLS) would make the database refuse such a read.

## Options

1. **Convention plus tests** (today). Cheap, portable (SQLite in tests), the failure mode is a bug.
2. **RLS on tenant tables.** A policy `USING (organization_id = current_setting('app.org')::uuid)`,
   with the setting made by `SET LOCAL` at the start of each transaction.

## Decision

Keep option 1 as the default and document option 2 so a team that needs it can adopt it without a
redesign. Reasons for not defaulting to it:

- Every request and background task must set the organization on its connection, inside a
  transaction, or PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode leaks it to the next client.
- Migrations, the admin, system jobs and the audit chain (null organization) need a bypass role,
  which is one more privileged path to guard.
- Two code paths to test (SQLite without RLS, PostgreSQL with), and a measurable planner cost.

## If you adopt it

1. Run the application as a role without `BYPASSRLS` (the runtime role already differs from the
   owner; see ADR 13).
2. `ALTER TABLE <t> ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE <t> FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;` and one
   policy per table on `organization_id`, with `WITH CHECK` for writes.
3. Set `app.org` with `SET LOCAL` where `ActionContext` is built and in
   `OrganizationContextMiddleware`; a request without an organization sets it to the nil UUID so
   nothing matches.
4. Give system jobs a separate role with an explicit policy for rows whose organization is null.
5. Run `tests/test_tenant_isolation.py` and the conformance suite against PostgreSQL with RLS on.

Start with the tables that hold the most sensitive data (uploads, webhooks, API keys).


---

<!-- docs/en/adr/two-mcp-servers.md -->

# ADR 15: Two MCP servers, with different jobs

**Status:** accepted.

## Context

"An MCP server" was one idea with two audiences. An AI agent can be asked to **operate a running
product** for a person (read their notes, create an invoice), or to **build the product** (add a
resource, fix a bug). The risks, the identity and the lifetime differ.

## Decision

- **Platform MCP** (`/mcp`, in the deployed service). Tools are the actions marked for the `mcp`
  channel; identity is a person's API key or OAuth token; every call is audited; writes can be
  undone. It also serves `platform://actions`, `platform://scopes` and a behaviour prompt.
- **Development MCP** (`python -m devtools.mcp`, on the developer's machine, stdio). No identity: it
  reads the rulebook, the registries and the docs, scaffolds code, checks conventions and runs the
  gate. It writes only under `src/` and `tests/`, only on request, and is never mounted in a
  deployed service.

They share nothing at runtime. The development server reuses the same registries (actions, data
catalog) so what an agent learns about the code is what the platform enforces.

## Consequences

- A leaked development server is a local file-write capability, not access to customer data, because
  it has no database credentials of its own beyond the developer's local settings.
- The platform server's attack surface does not grow with developer tooling.
- The development server's tools are the first thing to update when a convention changes: they read
  `src/devtools/conventions.py`, the same source as `AGENTS.md`.
